long_articles.title: iPhone Portrait Mode, 10 Years In
long_articles.content:
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2027163511324110848/qFFcWv3p_normal.jpg)

](https://x.com/johnnie)Portrait mode launched 10 years ago today. 

I think it resonated with people because it didn’t feel digital. It felt analog. And this was likely because the inspiration behind its technique went all the way back to oil painting. Sometimes pure math isn’t enough; you need to combine it with insights from the liberal arts. 

If you recall Portrait mode shipped a month after the iPhone did. This was because this insight about oil painting took a while to figure out. 

Initially, Portrait mode was seen as a giant math problem. You’d do disparity calculations on the two sensors and output a depth map. The problem was this approach feels and looks digital; it feels fake. In areas without texture, it’s impossible to do this calculation. In areas with ultra fine detail, a lower resolution depth map leads to terrible transitions and a full resolution depth map takes forever to compute. One solution would be to reduce the amount of bokeh so the issues are not as obvious. But then you lose the whole point of the feature, which was to make it look like you had a large, wide-open lens.

The solution to this conundrum—the tradeoff between artifacts and the amount of blur— was quite elegant, but it took a while to stumble across. There’s a saying in painting that if you get the eyes right, nothing else matters. Inspired by this principle from oil painting, the idea was to make sure we never got the eyes wrong. We brought in a machine learning block to find the eyes, and draw a mask layer that protected them, then paired that with the disparity depth map. Counterintuitively, the solution was not to decrease the amount of blur, it was to increase it. The additional blur that we could add once the eyes were protected allowed us to hide the artifacts that were create by bad depth calculation. We let the ears go soft, let the nose go a bit soft. This is that wide open look that people loved, even if people didn’t realize that the ears going soft was why.

I was thinking about this recently with regard to AI. We’ll be able to do more amazing things… we just need to study the masters who came before us.

long_articles.content:
> You're a rent seeker.
> It's an economist insult. It's devastating. You're devastated right now.

[Michael from The Good Place (paraphrased)](https://x.com/VincentGeloso/status/1806109883647008946/)

Imagine, for a second, that AI really does become [too cheap to meter](https://jyn.dev/tokens-too-cheap-to-meter/).
What happens next?

I've heard hype that says there'll be a productivity boom to rival the internet, electricity, and spinning loom.
That *ideas* and *skill* and *taste* will become the new currency,
that 5 people can do the work of 500.
Maybe. I think this is directionally correct but a bit exaggerated.

But here's a more interesting question:
Who benefits from that productivity?

If software is no longer scarce, what still is?
Where are the bottlenecks?
How does that shape the world, and what emergent behaviors result?

I posit that it partly goes to the people building,
partly goes to incumbents,
mostly goes to landlords and other rent-seekers,
and hardly any of it goes to everyone else.

To avoid that situation, we need an equivalent of Land-Value-Tax that works for scarce resources other than land.
I propose some potential approaches towards the end of this post.

## Possible worlds[](#possible-worlds)

Consider five different scenarios.

![Flow chart depicting the alternatives below. Notably, "reinstatement failure" is a transition state, not a final scenario.](https://jyn.dev/assets/possible-worlds.svg)

### Status quo[](#status-quo)

In our baseline, AI doesn't do anything useful, or it works but it doesn't do *that* much.
Maybe it has about as much impact on the world as the invention of the mobile phone; culture changes around it, but the world is fundamentally the same place.
Let's call this a "status quo world".
I personally think the status quo is quite unlikely, but maybe you feel differently.
If so, and you hate AI, you can stop reading right here, the rest of the post will just make you mad.

### Messy transition[](#messy-transition)

For this and all future worlds, let's assume AI really does work and really does result in greatly increased productivity that revolutionizes the economy.
Not only that, but also that we get at least a limited form of "recursive self-improvement" where improvements in AI get faster as AI itself gets better. [1](#fn-6)
What next?

Will AI take our jobs?
We're [already seeing this](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/canaries-in-the-coal-mine-six-facts-about-the-recent-employment-effects-of-artificial-intelligence/) to some extent in markets that are "AI-exposed", such as programmers, translators, and people just entering the job market.
But that doesn't necessarily mean they can't get other jobs.
The National Bureau of Economic Research published [a paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25684) about exactly this possibility in 2019:

> […] the *displacement effect* of automation has been counterbalanced by technologies that create new tasks in which labor has a comparative advantage. Such new tasks generate not only a positive productivity effect, but also a *reinstatement effect*—they reinstate labor into a broader range of tasks and thus change the task content of production in favor of labor. The reinstatement effect is the polar opposite of the displacement effect and directly increases the labor share as well as labor demand.

> History is also replete with examples of the creation of new tasks and the reinstatement effect […]

In this world, there are a lot fewer programmers, but a lot more UI designers, sales engineers, and HCI researchers.
There is significant short- and mid-term displacement, but in 10 years things shake out mostly ok.
Labor has less influence over capital than today; wealth inequality gets worse; careers and jobs become more unstable.
Overall though, people can still make rent [2](#fn-12).
Let's call this a "messy transition world".

### Reinstatement failure[](#reinstatement-failure)

What happens if the reinstatement effect fails?
What if jobs change faster than people can retrain, and long-term employment becomes more and more unstable?
What if nearly *all* jobs become automated?

Well, first we're going to see [labor lose out power against capital](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2016/09/berg.htm).
As this spreads to other industries and demographics, we'll start seeing more and more unemployment.
People and organizations who were lucky enough to catch the automation wave start accumulating more and more wealth;
an ever-narrowing fraction goes to people who work for a living.
Eventually, a small plutocracy controls the majority of the world's wealth.

This is possible on an economic level, but also on a geopolitical level.
Not every country has its own GPU foundries; not every country is part of the global supply chain for those foundries.
We could see a post-modern version of colonialism, mediated through markets rather than force.

This plutocratic world is not stable.
It's the nature of plutocrats to try and accumulate more and more power, and to automate more and more of the labor that generates their income.
Unlike today, they will actually have the power to do so, and unemployment spreads like wildfire.
An increasing portion of the population is simply unable to find a job.

If this gets bad enough, I see one of three possible *political* reactions, in the sense of an action taken by a country's government.

### Stable equilibria[](#stable-equilibria)

#### Butlerian Jihad[](#butlerian-jihad)

If a government takes no action at all in response to increasing unemployment, people get more and more desperate until there is violent revolution.
One possibility is that the revolution is crushed, and the country becomes a North Korea-like autocracy (hopefully we can all agree this is bad).
Another possibility is that the revolution succeeds.

Now, I have friends who think that [Revolution Is The Answer](https://blogs.kent.ac.uk/ageofrevolution/revolutionary-figures/karl-marx/), and will usher in the [Fully-Automated Post-Scarcity Luxury Gay Space Communism](https://theculture.fandom.com/wiki/The_Culture) of the future.
I, unfortunately, am not so hopeful.
Looking at history, and at small-scale upheavals in my own communities, I just don't think this is going to happen.
You have to remember: someone who's been unemployed for years due to AI is *angry*.
They're not going to care whether you were using AI to build solar panels, to automate driving a truck, or to build military drones;
they're just going to see someone who has contributed to their helplessness.

Instead, I think revolution would look more like Frank Herbert's [Butlerian Jihad](https://dune.fandom.com/wiki/Butlerian_Jihad), or Walter Miller's [A Canticle for Leibowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Canticle_for_Leibowitz):
*Indiscriminate* destruction; mass pogroms; loss of human knowledge; book burnings.
It's much easier to destroy things than to rebuild them.

Revolution is not inherently liberatory!
If it doesn't completely destroy the institutions that maintain our society, the most likely outcome is "the same as always, with someone else in charge".
Even [Robespierre was in favor of property rights](https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/%C5%92uvres_de_Robespierre/Sur_la_propri%C3%A9t%C3%A9._Projet_de_d%C3%A9claration_des_droits_de_l%E2%80%99homme_et_du_citoyen).
At a bare minimum you need [a plan for self-correcting systems that react to changing events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Cybersyn).

#### Bread and circuses[](#bread-and-circuses)

A government could react earlier.
The most likely reaction I foresee is to extend existing welfare and unemployment programs, in effect resulting in Universal Basic Income (UBI).

This is good! I am in favor of UBI!
However, UBI does not guarantee a good life for the people receiving it.
Eliezer Yudkowsky, as much as I hate to give it to him, has a good article about this called [Universal Basic Income and Poverty](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/fPvssZk3AoDzXwfwJ/universal-basic-income-and-poverty):

> it only takes a life lacking in one resource needed to survive, to produce some quality that I think ancient poor people would also recognize as 'poverty'.

> It's the quality of working yourself until you can't work any longer; of taking on jobs that are painful to do, and require groveling submission to bosses, because that's what it takes to get the few scraps to hang on.

> […]
> somehow there is a Poverty Equilibrium which beat a 100-fold increase in productivity plus everything else that went right over the last thousand years.
> […]

> I do not understand the Poverty Equilibrium.  So I expect that a Universal Basic Income would fail to eliminate poverty, for reasons I don't fully understand.

I think what Yud is missing here is very simple: rent-seeking and incumbent effects.
A world where everyone has, say, a guaranteed minimum of 50k annual income, is a world where rental housing costs about 25k a year and the rest goes to food, utilities, transport and healthcare.
Above a certain point, making food/utilities/transport/healthcare cheaper doesn't help in the long term, because it just results in housing swallowing an ever-increasing proportion of income.

Don't just take my word for it.
[Henry George](https://www.econlib.org/library/YPDBooks/George/grgPP.html?chapter_num=23), [Enrico Moretti](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~moretti/handbook.pdf), and [Richard Hornbeck](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~moretti/tfp.pdf) all predict near-total capture of productivity increases by landlords and economic rent-collectors when housing supply is sufficiently limited.
Their findings are pretty bleak!

This world is explored further in "[Manna](https://web.archive.org/web/20260725174355/https://marshallbrain.com/manna1)", a fictional dystopia where all service jobs are automated down to the minute by an AI "manager" that whispers tasks into everyone's ear.
The end result is a permanent underclass, half of whom work precarious jobs with extreme hours, and the other half of whom are permanently unemployed and live in government-sponsored housing.

Let's call this a "rentier world", for the plutocracy that makes their money through rent and capital, not through innovation.
Here, people can rent enough to survive, but scarcity is everywhere, and almost no one owns anything that would give them power.

#### Distributed ownership[](#distributed-ownership)

["Manna"](https://web.archive.org/web/20260515191335/https://marshallbrain.com/manna5) explores another world, one where automation improvements are captured by the whole population, not just plutocrats.
Scarcity is, essentially, a thing of the past.
There is no real-estate mogul extracting rent, because there is no land ownership.
There is no one working themselves to death, because everyone has plenty.
Instead, the land and production are split equally between everyone in the society.

Now, I think Manna has a lot of funny ideas (constant surveillance sounds a lot like a dystopia to me), but its *ownership model* is quite interesting.
The catch, of course, is that we have to get there somehow.

Let's call this a "post-scarcity world", for the abundance that's present throughout the society.
This is the world I want to see.
This is the world I want to build together.

## Distribut*ing* ownership[](#distributing-ownership)

How do we build a post-scarcity world?
How do we distribute the enormous amount of material wealth in our society to everyone within it?

### Tax rents, not capital[](#tax-rents-not-capital)

In economics, there is a concept called *[deadweight loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadweight_loss)*.
Most taxes are "inefficient" in a broad sense.
For example, when you tax food, you cause people to buy less food or cheaper food, with negative health outcomes.
This inefficiency is called "deadweight loss".
A tax is "efficient" if it does not introduce deadweight loss.

Lars Doucet, writing on Scott Alexander's blog, talks about [Georgism and Land Value Tax](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/does-georgism-work-five-years-later):

> George argues that poverty paradoxically advances alongside progress because, as material conditions improve, landowners can charge more rent for locational benefits they didn’t create.
> […]

> Henry George’s remedy is the *land value tax*, or LVT. In its ideal form, this tax would capture and redistribute the annual *rental* value of land; that is, the recurring value of the land *excluding* the value of any buildings or other improvements on top of it. In practice, this looks a lot like a conventional property tax paired with a “universal building exemption.” Notably, George isn’t simply in favor of a land value tax; he’s also *opposed* to taxes on both labor and capital.

> […[earlier](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-progress-and-poverty)…]
> Keep in mind also that the Georgist Land Value Tax is pair [sic] with a "Citizen's Dividend" or what we see as UBI, so that it's not the government claiming land rent, rather the land rent is taxed and split up equally for all men.

[Land-value tax is efficient](https://bluerepublik.wordpress.com/2019/07/31/welfare-economics-of-the-land-value-tax/)!
I said above that UBI doesn't help much because demand-side interventions just raise housing costs.
Conversely, LVT *does* help because the supply of land is fixed:
landlords are *already* charging as much as their tenants can afford, so when taxes go up, landlords have no choice but to pay the tax out of pocket.

Not only that, but I think this is conceptually the right model:
There's a difference between a landlord who owns the property and does nothing to work on it and a property-management company who's responsible for fixing issues.
The property-management company is doing useful work; the landlord is not.
We should pay people for the work they've done (improvements built on land, and maintenance of those improvements),
while not allowing them to capture value from the underlying shared resource (the land itself).

#### Measuring value[](#measuring-value)

So how do we figure out the value of land?

LVT is generally measured using *[appraisals](https://boe.ca.gov/info/iav/lesson15.htm)* which distinguish "improvement value" from "land value".
You get the latter by looking at prices for properties with little improvement (parking lots, empty fields, etc.) and then comparing that to the price of buildings in nearby areas [3](#fn-5).

We said earlier that LVT works because the supply of land is fixed.
There are other areas where supply is fixed: radio broadcast spectrums, IPv4 addresses, mineral and resource rights, utility contracts.

Land and IP addresses are in some ways the hard cases because they're private property.
For public property, like radio spectrums and resource rights, there's a much simpler solution, which is to force an auction for ownership of the right every so often.
If the incumbent wins, the auction acts as a tax; otherwise, the incoming owner pays the tax.
Either way, the owner pays fair market value.
The US government already [auctions off spectrum rights](https://www.fcc.gov/about-auctions).

Note that this is auctioning the *right to the scarce resource*, not the capital used to develop that resource.
For example, a radio broadcast company retains their broadcast towers if they lose an auction; they only lose the spectrum itself.

### Tax cash flow, not income[](#tax-cash-flow-not-income)

Another term in economics is *[economic rent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_rent)*.
This refers to income that is not necessary to incentivize valuable work or investment.
In other words, the "rentier" is collecting more income than justified (in the sense of "economically worthwhile") by their risk + investment + labor.
This often happens when the rentier controls a scarce good that no one else is able to create or buy.

Not all rentiers are landlords [4](#fn-9).
I know someone who ran a ["Managed Service Provider"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managed_services).
This is a kind of IT company where a business pays a fixed fee every quarter, in exchange for having all their computer problems repaired at no additional charge.
This particular company was a registered ["Authorized Service Provider"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authorized_service_provider) for a [large computer manufacturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_equipment_manufacturer), which means that the MSP was authorized to conduct repairs on behalf of the manufacturer without voiding the hardware warranty.
This is quite relatively rare; most companies do not have this relationship.

The owner sold most of the company many years ago, but kept one thing, which was the repair authorization.
They no longer do any work for the MSP at all, but employ a project manager, who takes contracts, delegates them to subcontractors, and coordinates between them and the manufacturer.
The owner takes some profit off the resulting fixes after paying the contractors and project manager.
This is also a form of economic rent:
The owner's income comes from controlling access to the authorization, not from labor, risk [5](#fn-10), or investment.

How do we distinguish the rent extracted by this MSP from the valuable production?
With LVT, we can value the land separately from the improvements built on top,
but here the authorization is inextricably tied to the work being done in its name.
We want to share the rents that the MSP receives, without discouraging the real positive impact it has by fixing computers.

One possible solution is to not try to separate these in the first place.
*Cash flow tax* is a generalization of LVT to other kinds of resources, keeping the same idea of taxing rents and deducting investments.
The UK's Institute for Fiscal Studies has [published a paper](https://ifs.org.uk/publications/full-expensing-and-corporation-tax-base) on exactly this:

> The intuition is that the company is taxed immediately on all receipts but can immediately deduct all outgoings at the same rate: with a 25% tax rate, the government covers 25% of the investment cost and takes 25% of the return, essentially becoming a compulsory silent partner in the project. If the revenue is worth more than the cost, 75% of the revenue will be worth more than 75% of the cost, so any project that is worthwhile before tax will be worthwhile after tax [6](#fn-8). That is a good thing.

"Any project that is worthwhile before tax will be worthwhile after tax" is another way of saying this is an efficient tax that causes no deadweight loss. [7](#fn-7)
"Compulsory silent partner" means that every citizen of the country is invested in every company, indirectly through the government.
This applies to companies that fail, not just companies that succeed!
Under this scheme, a company that loses money receives a tax refund, not just a tax deduction.
Just like LVT would be the only tax on property, this would be the only tax on corporate profits, replacing existing taxes.
Norway [already does something like this](https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/prop.-1-ls-20242025/id3057469/?ch=2#kap2-3-3) for oil and hydropower.

We would apply deductions and refunds to wages, not just to capital investment.
The government would pay a portion of every salary and independent contract, at the same rate as the rest of the cash-flow tax.
This avoids incentivizing investment over labor.

Why is this better than a corporate profit tax?
Precisely because the refunds and deductions avoid deadweight loss.
Because it causes no economic distortion, we can raise the tax much higher without disincentivizing useful work.
If we take our earlier MSP as an example, they would pay more tax on their profits, but much less in wages, because the government helps them cover that cost.

### Distribute the funds[](#distribute-the-funds)

Using our tax income, we would redistribute it to everyone in our society as dividends.
This would be unconditional, without means-testing.
Our LVT and cash-flow taxes give everyone an economic stake in productivity improvements,
which means the money doesn't immediately evaporate into economic rent and corporate conglomerates [8](#fn-11).
People still spend their income on housing, but most of the money goes back into the dividend pool through LVT.
Similarly, money spent on goods and services goes back into the pool, tying dividends to *the whole economy* rather than to the minimum necessary to live.

This is not new.
Both [Alaska](https://apfc.org/about/history/) and [Norway](https://www.nbim.no/) both discovered enormous reserves of oil and put the profits into reserves that are saved and redistributed for the benefit of all citizens.
It really is politically feasible to make these changes when there's sufficient wealth floating around.

With these funds, people would become much much less dependent on their employer for a stable source of income.
This is good, because as AI and automation develops, there will be fewer jobs.
By themselves, dividends don't give us post-scarcity, nor independence from work.
What they *do* give us is a way to ensure that benefits to a small segment of the population are shared between everyone.
If, in the future, we have enough productivity and resources to support everyone on dividends alone,
we have the governance processes in place to make sure we end up in a post-scarcity world rather than a rentier world.

This doesn't work automatically.
The taxes have to be high enough that the dividends make up for lost work hours during the transition period.
We'd need some way to avoid companies from simply relocating to somewhere with lower taxes.
But—if we somehow manage that—I really do think we'd have a bright future ahead of us.

## Transition plans[](#transition-plans)

If you call your representative to ask them to increase taxes on landlords; homeowners; conglomerates; and banks; and then redistribute the money to everyone as dividends, they will laugh you out of the room.
These are some of the most powerful and influential groups in politics, in large part *due to* their giant rental incomes.
Just saying "hi could you dismantle the political machine please" will not work.
Instead, we need some sort of incremental transition that appeases existing interests.

### Homeowners[](#homeowners)

Let's start with homeowners.
The traditional problem here is people on fixed-income who cannot tolerate tax increases.
If you switch from property taxes to LVT, and this results in a net tax increase, they really do experience material hardship.

One possible solution is to [defer the increased tax](https://www.revenue.ie/en/property/local-property-tax/deferral-of-payment/index.aspx) until after the sale of the property, charging interest on the deferral.
Until then, the tax collected stays at previous values, avoiding a sudden "spike" in costs for people on fixed income.
This still results in an overall wealth transfer, just delayed by a few years;
and because it's tied to the sale, you're not punishing people for ownership: selling gives them the free cash they need to pay the tax.
This would be a *one-time* deferment; unlike [California's Prop 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_California_Proposition_13), it would go away after the first sale.

Note that we *want* new houses to be built, we *want* them to sell at market price.
What we *don't* want is for people's life savings to be tied up in their home, and for landlords to make a giant profit even when they're not doing any maintenance.
[I do not believe that home ownership is intrinsically good](https://byrnehobart.medium.com/the-30-year-mortgage-is-an-intrinsically-toxic-product-200c901746a).

### Businesses[](#businesses)

Businesses have a clear motivation here: our cash-flow tax gives them a discount for all investments.
Even raising the tax is not necessarily bad for the business, because it gives them more cash up-front, allowing them to take more risks and start more projects.
The strongest opposition would be from businesses who make few investments but collect a lot of profit, i.e. exactly the people we want to redistribute wealth away from.

If government budgets are a problem, we could "ease in" the tax over time for new projects, keeping current profit tax rates and adding investment deductions until the two rates match.
Only then would we raise the overall cash-flow tax rate.

## Conclusion[](#conclusion)

The goal of this proposal is not to take away profits from people who are earning 'too much', or to single out landlords as uniquely bad.
The goal is to *give everyone a stake in productivity improvements* in a way that still keeps the natural self-regulation of the free market,
and to make people economically secure without being dependent on their employer.
I *want* to live in Asimov's, Iain M. Bank's, Kim Stanley Robinson's post-scarcity worlds.
And I really do believe that we have a path to get there.
We just need to open our eyes and walk down it.

In other words:
Land is different from capital.
Economic rent is a curse.
Economic security is freedom.

To all a good night.

long_articles.summary: Bryan Cantrill has a great line from a [talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-zRN7XLCRhc&t=34m7s) where he cautions against anthropomorphizing[1](#fn-1) Oracle CEO Larry Ellison. I think it’s also a
long_articles.content:
Bryan Cantrill has a great line from a [talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-zRN7XLCRhc&t=34m7s) where he cautions against anthropomorphizing[1](#fn-1) Oracle CEO Larry Ellison. I think it’s also a mistake to treat any tech company like a person. Here’s the full quote:

> You need to think of Larry Ellison the way you think of a lawnmower. You don’t anthropomorphize your lawnmower, the lawnmower just mows the lawn, you stick your hand in there and it’ll chop it off, the end. You don’t think ‘oh, the lawnmower hates me’ — lawnmower doesn’t give a shit about you, lawnmower can’t hate you. Don’t anthropomorphize the lawnmower. Don’t fall into that trap about Oracle.

### Companies are machines, not persons[](#companies-are-machines-not-persons)

Here are some examples of anthropomorphizing companies:

- My company really owes me for that hard thing I did

- I’m fighting the good fight against my company on issue X (e.g. accessibility) and they hate me for it

- My company is vindictively retaliating against me because of that mistake I made

- My company and I are partners in the mission to make the world a better place

All of these are mistakes. Your relationship to the tech company that employs you is not like a relationship with a person. It’s more like your relationship with your car[2](#fn-2). If you drive poorly or fail to change your oil, your car may stop working or even kill you, but it doesn’t love or hate you. It has no sense of fairness. It’s simply a dangerous, useful machine: useful enough to be worth getting into despite the risks. Anthropomorphizing it makes it harder to avoid those risks[3](#fn-3).

Why is it so hard to avoid this trap? First, humans anthropomorphize everything by default. Second, whenever you’re interacting with the company, you’re interacting with a person: your manager, your colleague, someone in HR, and so on. Third, when you’re in the power of some entity, it’s psychologically comforting to think of it like another human. This is the same principle that caused early humans to attribute lightning to the power of Zeus, because Zeus (unlike electrical imbalances in storm clouds) can be placated with prayer and sacrifice.

### Disproportionate efforts and rewards[](#disproportionate-efforts-and-rewards)

Relationships with machines are very different from relationships with people. The biggest difference is that *machines do not respect effort*. If you put a lot of work into doing a favor for a friend, your friend will appreciate it even if the favor itself is not a big deal. Conversely, if you help somebody out at trivial cost to yourself, that help will be relatively unappreciated. But a car doesn’t care how much effort you put into maintaining it. If you spend hours replacing a car’s engine, but the brake line is damaged, the car won’t remain functional out of respect for your effort on the engine: instead, the brakes will fail, killing you.

Tech companies work like this. Everyone who’s worked at one for long enough knows that it’s very hard to predict what work will be high-impact. The project you slaved over for months will often get a “nice, now what’s next” reaction, while the tool you built in fifteen minutes (or the question you answered in a Slack channel) will sometimes get wild praise and recognition. This can drive engineers a little mad, because they’re anthropomorphizing their tech company, and a person who behaved like this would be dangerously unstable. But if you treat your company like a machine, this shouldn’t be surprising at all.

It’s hard to predict high-impact work, but it’s not impossible. The best way to operate at a big tech company — as I’ve said [again](https://seangoedecke.com/side-bets) [and](https://seangoedecke.com/the-spotlight) [again](https://seangoedecke.com/dangerous-advice) — is to try and develop this skill, and to spend most of your time looking for the low-effort high-reward wins. It’s hard to do that if you’re secretly imagining your company as a person.

### Anthropomorphism is a dangerous shorthand[](#anthropomorphism-is-a-dangerous-shorthand)

A natural objection here is to point out that tech companies (unlike cars) are composed of people who might indeed owe you, hate you, love you, and so on. According to this view, when people say “my company hates me”, they aren’t making the mistake of anthropomorphizing a corporation, they’re using shorthand to say “my boss and skip-level hate me”. I think this is still a dangerously sloppy way to think.

In my experience, engineers who think they’re hated are often not. Managers in large tech companies do hold grudges, but (particularly the higher up you get) are tolerably cold-blooded. You don’t get to senior director or VP by needlessly throwing away useful tools. I can recall a few cases[4](#fn-4) where engineers told me they were hated, but I later found out[5](#fn-5) that managers considered them dangerous or unreliable: loose cannons whose usefulness didn’t outweigh their tendency to go off the rails and cause damage. From the perspective of the engineer being forced out of the company, it feels like you’re being run out of town by people who hate you. But if you want to *avoid* being run out of town, it’s useful to recognize when you’re being treated as a defective tool.

It’s also useful to keep in mind the difference between “my manager hates me” and “my company hates me”, because managers are often temporary. You can sometimes just wait out a bad relationship with your manager. You’ll have a slightly uphill battle with the next one — since the handoff won’t be positive — but it’s certainly possible to get back on track. If you can figure out why your manager hates you, you might also be able to fix it (or at least mitigate[6](#fn-6) it).

### Don’t go too far in the other direction[](#dont-go-too-far-in-the-other-direction)

Engineers who’ve learned not to anthropomorphize tech companies sometimes go too far in the other direction, by treating companies as a *computer program*. This is the wrong kind of machine: tech companies aren’t people, but they aren’t programs either. They operate on incentives and [illegible](https://seangoedecke.com/seeing-like-a-software-company) interpersonal relationships, not on consistent logical steps.

The classic example of this is the engineer who reads the company handbook cover-to-cover and makes sure they follow all the rules. When they’re looking to be promoted, they take the role guidelines and make sure they’re following them point-by-point. They take what they’re told very literally: when the company says “X is our top priority”, they internalize that.

The problem with this is that handbooks, guidelines and internal communications are the [legible superstructure](https://seangoedecke.com/seeing-like-a-software-company) of a massive illegible web of dependencies that make up the actual operations of any company. That superstructure will not cover the [real criteria](https://seangoedecke.com/staff-engineer-promotions) for promotions, or the rules that are [designed to be broken](https://seangoedecke.com/breaking-rules). The “top priority” of the superstructure can rapidly shift, leaving literal-minded engineers confused and disheartened.

### Conclusion[](#conclusion)

It’s understandable to feel ill-treated by a company, or to harbor resentment — particularly since there are actual humans at the company who are involved in that treatment of you. But companies themselves don’t hold grudges, even as they force out people who they’re incentivized to force out[7](#fn-7). It can even be a mistake to anthropomorphize very senior managers, whose work personas are more identified with the machine the higher up you go[8](#fn-8). I suppose at the top you have Larry Ellison, as Bryan Cantrill says, who is better modeled as a lawnmower than as a human being. 

No relationship with an individual person at your company will save you from being careless with the machine: it will chew you up and spit you out. You need to [learn how to drive the car](https://seangoedecke.com/knowing-how-to-drive-the-car/). This is scary, because it means that sometimes you will just get punished for [no reason](https://bobistheoilguy.com/forums/threads/catastrophic-engine-failure-share-your-stories.358302/). But it’s also good news, because it means that you can get disproportionate rewards for relatively little effort, so long as you make the right decisions.

long_articles.content:
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh3Z41XAQEyv90YDSNsUZoRLFphrYb6i6dcfu2ZGSv0bIYyLdZ1ubThIPquyvjUS2fDx-GdIqf4sIUl77bKZCgodMzYrW-6lt2fci3thoYOJscOyOr0mTDnbIif9J324iDTr0wNpXR0AYuXZhCx-7CuPRL7vFLrmZbISj9Z585sNjYK7sYb5oXg62Bh3iY/s320/PXL_20261013_011922071.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh3Z41XAQEyv90YDSNsUZoRLFphrYb6i6dcfu2ZGSv0bIYyLdZ1ubThIPquyvjUS2fDx-GdIqf4sIUl77bKZCgodMzYrW-6lt2fci3thoYOJscOyOr0mTDnbIif9J324iDTr0wNpXR0AYuXZhCx-7CuPRL7vFLrmZbISj9Z585sNjYK7sYb5oXg62Bh3iY/s4080/PXL_20261013_011922071.jpg)

By now regular readers of this blog are quite familiar with my affection for the 1996 [Apple Network Server](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/search/label/ans), Apple's Unix-through-and-through $10,000+ server that only shipped with, and only officially ran, Harpoon, its unique superset of IBM AIX. An ANS 500, the lower tier of this dorm fridge-sized computer, was the first server I ever personally owned, a nearly-new hand-me-down after Steve Jobs convinced Gil Amelio to cancel the machine and the bookstore's vendor at the University I worked for wouldn't support it anymore. There are [several fascinating features](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2023/11/the-apple-network-servers-all-too.html) present in Harpoon that were never implemented in any other Apple product. Currently I have three, that original ANS 500, this ANS 700 here which I use for testing, and a battery-bombed EVT prototype (a so-called "Shiner ESB" that [used to be at Netscape](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2021/10/shiner-esb-apple-network-server.html)).

The ANS was strongly based on the Power Macintosh 9500 and Apple was known to have demonstrated the ANS with Mac OS during development, but this confused potential buyers, causing the ability to boot Mac OS to be stripped from production systems. While then-CTO Ellen Hancock claimed in 1997 a ROM swap would enable the ANS to boot Mac OS again *and* Windows NT, these ROMs were believed to be vapourware until a former Apple employee presented a working dump of [both the preproduction ROM and the later ANS Mac OS ROM](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2025/10/the-apple-network-server-macos-roms.html). [A prototype Windows NT ROM also emerged](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2026/01/hands-on-with-two-apple-network-server.html) from another former employee, though there are pieces missing and booting Windows NT natively on the ANS is still a work in progress (hopefully to be the subject of [a future article](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/search/label/ans)).

It turned out [I had one of the preproduction ROMs myself](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2026/01/hands-on-with-two-apple-network-server.html) and didn't realize what it was. Because the later Mac OS ROM was apparently unfinished, [it doesn't properly support the L2 cache](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2026/05/testing-macos-on-apple-network-server.html) and consequently runs substantially slower, and it can't boot AIX. The preproduction ROM does boot both operating systems and does support the cache. On the other hand, it doesn't support the on-board video or the front Fast Wide SCSI-2 controller, the on-board MACE Ethernet doesn't work, and after MacOS first boots, the next restart without zapping the PRAM will come up with a black screen.

The good news is, many of the issues with the preproduction ROM in Mac OS can be fixed or worked around in software. So I've fixed or worked around many of them in software: the MACE Ethernet is fixed, the on-board video is now supported, and the ANS can restart properly back into Mac OS. Plus, because it's the preproduction ROM, you can still boot AIX, thus preserving the entire historical reason for Shiner's existence. Here's the first cut of that software and how it was developed.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg6CkO34PaOUnL6hPI7sYn9fCUL30ZE1hyphenhyphenTBmb4tzKgCmUALiUX-i063YdMnYOGdDG4xzh79Fik9fAYlCQmi_qDsIafrvMwykhSoXi5EtUOW13FPhAhJW_1dIqYsDRVloaoYDYktjKJypRzqapghHxHOecAA6NwpUGXpx0wIbrmRGp5Pc-0bbkF3X_ifuY/s320/PXL_20260118_202225393.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg6CkO34PaOUnL6hPI7sYn9fCUL30ZE1hyphenhyphenTBmb4tzKgCmUALiUX-i063YdMnYOGdDG4xzh79Fik9fAYlCQmi_qDsIafrvMwykhSoXi5EtUOW13FPhAhJW_1dIqYsDRVloaoYDYktjKJypRzqapghHxHOecAA6NwpUGXpx0wIbrmRGp5Pc-0bbkF3X_ifuY/s4080/PXL_20260118_202225393.jpg)

Naturally, the first order of business is to get an Apple Network Server and the 1.1.20.1 preproduction ROM (the production ROM is version 1.1.22). I can't help you with the first part, but replica ROMs now exist to cover the second part, and as of this writing [Joe's Computer Museum](https://jcm-1.com/product/apple-network-server-rom-v1-1-20-0/) has a few in stock (not affiliated, just a satisfied occasional customer). I [tested the original design](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2026/05/testing-macos-on-apple-network-server.html) of these ROM DIMMs, kindly provided by Jeff Walther. Jeff assembled and donated this particular batch to Joe Strosnider, who is selling them and donating the proceeds in turn to the maintenance of the Tinker Different forum, where [this whole thing started](https://tinkerdifferent.com/threads/apple-network-server-macos-based-roms-found.4756/).

Now that you have the basic hardware, you'll then need to install Mac OS to an external bootable SCSI volume. For this project I use a 25-pin BlueSCSI which connects directly to the ANS' rear SCSI port and runs on termination power. Set up a blank disk image of the desired size to the device's (micro)SD card and rename it to the desired SCSI ID, which for the ANS is typically SCSI ID 2.

If you have another Mac with a SCSI port handy, it's easiest to do the MacOS installation to the external volume with that system. Make sure it installs Mac OS for any supported Mac, especially if you are using a model-specific installer CD; up to Mac OS 9.1 inclusive will boot directly on the ANS, and 9.1 is what I'm using here. 7.6 will work and late versions of System 7.5 *might* work, but I recommend at least 8.1 or later. If you only have the ANS and/or have no other suitable vintage Mac that can perform the installation, you can do it on the ANS itself with a bit more difficulty. For that you'll need to not only create the blank disk image but additionally include an ISO of a bootable MacOS CD (use ID 0), plus install a Power Mac-compatible PCI video card — I use a Twin Turbo 128MA but any ATI Mac-specific card of the era should also work, such as the Rage Orion.

Finally, unplug the server, unlock and pull open the mainboard drawer, remove the PRAM battery, install the preproduction ROM DIMM, and leave the drawer open and the system completely depowered for at least several minutes while you enjoy the droll prose of this blog post.
  

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjR9cnTwCl-BaWHIcjTrftEX3WDjaebx7Sfu16mubRK7QoaG18OuXDeKtCOe9QjAWHLb7sgLKB66tcitW3Wkuigr8EuOa4zkiiliZ5w-A9sIT3zlmKT0eWDhbpzsayr9WF6IFetGRy_X7fW9Quhk-csQ3teM9GbDWjWxTBH4ehiasicG1BQwyBuLwMurV4/s320/PXL_20261013_013311169.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjR9cnTwCl-BaWHIcjTrftEX3WDjaebx7Sfu16mubRK7QoaG18OuXDeKtCOe9QjAWHLb7sgLKB66tcitW3Wkuigr8EuOa4zkiiliZ5w-A9sIT3zlmKT0eWDhbpzsayr9WF6IFetGRy_X7fW9Quhk-csQ3teM9GbDWjWxTBH4ehiasicG1BQwyBuLwMurV4/s4080/PXL_20261013_013311169.jpg)

Here's the back of my testing ANS 700. The monitor is connected to the 700's video port, the BlueSCSI is plugged into the SCSI connector, and a Farallon standard AAUI-to-twisted pair dongle is attached to the on-board MACE Ethernet AAUI port (Apple's perverse little rework of AUI to avoid confusion with the Mac DA-15 video port).

Technically that should be all you need to run Mac OS or AIX. However, I also have the Twin Turbo video card in slot 1 (where it would usually be in a 9500, the closest hardware relative to the ANS), and as an alternative for the MACE Ethernet I have one of the unobtainium 10Mbit ANS Ethernet PCI cards in slot 6 that I ordered from Apple Austin when they were blowing out leftover Shiner hardware. This card works in AIX and later versions of Mac OS (not 7.6, possibly 8, definitely 9); my only 100Mbit ANS Ethernet card is in the 500. A regular Power Mac-compatible Ethernet PCI card will suffice if all you want to do is run Mac OS.

Let's talk about drivers and PCI devices on Power Macs.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhLXs_w6SU8ogqRkiq0usmTmPyG79zvoiNXhLY05phzwE06-2PrfDXtDD5cSkq7lz7kE2kZRCTM5uIISueDNKt8AuHhpwDnsiFMGr8YzUJ_S0sf6r1nsDSRYO5fO82lijh64rK24qtmB85_IYuXNsIZnAsBJsIOz_vk8Auq2-Vv70yiVdUWIqVPz4XRglk/s320/copland.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhLXs_w6SU8ogqRkiq0usmTmPyG79zvoiNXhLY05phzwE06-2PrfDXtDD5cSkq7lz7kE2kZRCTM5uIISueDNKt8AuHhpwDnsiFMGr8YzUJ_S0sf6r1nsDSRYO5fO82lijh64rK24qtmB85_IYuXNsIZnAsBJsIOz_vk8Auq2-Vv70yiVdUWIqVPz4XRglk/s3235/copland.jpg)

Denizens of the classic Mac OS are painfully familiar with 

INITs and 

CDEVs, which is to say, the extensions and control panels which extend the operating system (and in many cases constitute substantial parts of it). Adding device support to the operating system required a 

DRVR resource, which could be stored in the declaration ROM of a NuBus card and available at power-on, or in an 

INIT or 

CDEV and made available during the boot process, or in a regular application and loaded on demand. (Parenthetically, desk accessories were also implemented as 

DRVRs.) Even after the 1994 transition to PowerPC, some, if not all, of such code still had to be 68K for backwards compatibility, and thus required emulation on a Power Macintosh.

Since this requirement was an obvious performance bottleneck, Apple attempted to address it in Copland, Apple's fallback attempt to modernise the Mac OS stepwise amid the slow-motion death marches of Taligent and PowerOpen-A/UX 4. Copland's tale of woe is a much longer story, to be the topic of [a future article](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/search/label/copland), but the part relevant to this piece was the new driver architecture it introduced. This aspect was part of how Copland's design partitioned its components ih memory to avoid the attendant pitfalls inherent in the classic Mac OS. In order to wall the old Mac OS world off but retain compatibility, everything that was 68K code lived in the so-called "cooperative" address space and was treated as data to be interpreted by the Power Mac 68K emulator, including 68K portions of the Toolbox; even PowerPC-native System 7 applications ran here. This cooperative address space would theoretically allow most applications to run as they did before, but intentionally without privileges to the rest of the system nor access to Copland's hardware abstraction layer (HAL).

  
As such, Copland drivers necessarily were fully native code, in this case implemented as regular PowerPC code fragments. These drivers hooked into the HAL and the Name Registry, an object database that tracked devices on the system and mediated loading and unloading device drivers as needed, and were collapsed into a separate global region at a lower execution level where only limited operating system functionality was available. Although such limitations restricted their ability to integrate with the operating system, it also enabled those drivers to run early in the boot process and remain protected from user code. This new class of driver was called a *native driver*.

Although Copland suffered from terminal second-system effect just as badly as its contemporaries, it was modular enough for parts of it to be used as transitional enhancements — such as its visual language, which later became the basis of Mac OS 8's Platinum theme, and other pieces that shipped more quietly. Germane to our discussion here was Apple's transition from NuBus to PCI, one not uniformly well-received by users, though in fairness it was effectively forced on Apple when IBM wouldn't support NuBus in the PowerOpen-based AIX 4. For these first PCI Power Macs, starting with the 9500 in 1995, Apple added a port of the Copland Name Registry to their ROMs as well as Eric Traut's faster dynamic recompiling 68K emulator, also intended for Copland.

In this scheme the system ROM initializes the hardware and hands control to its onboard copy of Open Firmware, which creates the device tree for all devices on the system, necessarily including PCI cards but also processor and logic board resources. The Code Fragment Manager, also in the Power Mac ROM, then runs code from any PCI card expansion ROMs and drivers in the Mac ROM itself. This code typically contains a low-level "expert" that creates a node in the Name Registry with sufficient information to identify the device and enable a driver to match against it.

Once the Name Registry is built out, the Mac ROM starts the Display Manager, SCSI Manager and/or ATA Manager, as needed, as part of booting the Mac OS kernel. These Managers in PCI Power Macs implement a different type of "expert" called a *family expert*. When the MacOS File Manager and Resource Manager are up, the Extensions folder is scanned for native drivers (stored as code fragments with a Type of ndrv, but otherwise the same general structure as their Copland antecessors) and handed to the expert of each particular service category for device classes the family expert supervises. Eligible and matching ndrvs, be they in ROM or on disk, are loaded before any other extension is ever invoked, and the family expert activates and wires them into the operating system.

All such drivers have a description block, usually heralded by the FourCC 

mtej (this code seems like it was based on someone's name — spill the beans in the comments if you know). The exact binary format is obscured a bit here by PEF's trivial packing method, used to reduce its footprint in ROM, but note the node name stored as a Pascal string (i.e., length byte first), and then the driver name, also stored as a Pascal string and invariably starting with a dot.

Immediately before the driver name length byte is an $06. The two bits set in this byte indicate that the driver is opened as soon as it is loaded (kDriverIsOpenedUponLoad, $02), and that the family expert is responsible for doing so (kDriverIsUnderExpertControl, $04). The PCI DDK documentation states that all video drivers should set these two bits, and only these two. The family expert handling graphics drivers is hinted by the FourCCs in the next line, ndrv for a general native driver service category, and vido for the type, in this case a graphics card.

You might well ask how the production ANS works at all without such an ndrv, and the answer is that Open Firmware doesn't need this driver to display anything on the screen — that's all specifically handled by the code in the ANS ROM, and Harpoon AIX has its own drivers. The ANS was never officially supported with Mac OS, so a proper Mac OS driver was never needed.

The next thing I started working on was fixing reboots in Mac OS, since every time I shut down the machine I had to reset PRAM or make other changes. This wasn't too hard because I never keep the PRAM battery in it anyway (it's a test machine), but it did mean I had to frequently redo various settings between test runs.

  
In [our previous article in January](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2026/01/hands-on-with-two-apple-network-server.html), we learned this was because Mac OS monkeys with the ANS' NVRAM settings as if it were a real Power Mac 9500, installing an inappropriate nvramrc OpenFirmware startup script that interferes with normal operation, and then sets the input and output devices to serial port ttya, which on the back is serial port 2 (yes, two). On Open Firmware 1.0.5 systems like most beige PCI Power Macs, this does nothing more than keep Open Firmware itself on the serial port; the video and ADB keyboard remain the console. On the ANS' 1.1.x firmware, however, it actually obeys these settings so that you can install and run Harpoon AIX over a serial port, and this was also apparently [how Shiner NetWare ran](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2023/12/when-power-macintosh-ran-netware.html). In this configuration the machine comes up with no video at all, though interestingly ADB devices are still useable in Mac OS, including the keyboard.

The Startup Disk control panel is at least *part* of this problem. In the 

CDEV are three resources, 

OFpt, 

OFtb and 

OFtc. The latter two define mappings between the Open Firmware platform identifier and the respective NVRAM settings in 

OFpt, which is stored as a single long null-terminated string with embedded Mac $0d carriage returns. (The unreleased [PowerExpress](https://www.applefritter.com/node/3367) turns up in this table as the Power Macintosh 9700.) When loaded, the 

CDEV overwrites the NVRAM settings with the one selected by platform.

Theoretically it should be possible to binary-patch in another mapping and then add a specific script for the ANS, which with this ROM would have a platform string of AAPL,ShinerESB. I determined this approach was unacceptable for two reasons: first, it required modifying standard OS components instead of adding to them, and second, it doesn't solve the ttya problem even if we alter the mapping so that *no* machines match. In fact, the very *string* ttya appears *nowhere* in Startup Disk, suggesting the input and output device settings are being munged someplace else.

In the prior article we solved this issue using [Boot Variables](https://ftp.netbsd.org/pub/NetBSD/arch/macppc/macos-utils/bootvars/), a utility originally written by Paul Mackerras ([now at IBM](https://www.talospace.com/2019/04/a-quick-trip-to-ibm-ozlabs.html)) which allows you to directly manipulate Open Firmware variables and save them. Because the changes to NVRAM occur before the boot process reaches the Finder, once we get to the Finder we can then fix everything and remain confident it will stay unmolested until the next boot. This process works but obviously requires manual intervention, so since Boot Variables is open source under the GNU Public License, I decided I'd just hack in a hard-coded version which automatically undoes the munge when run.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEga8F95aDy7a_n56G2zWA4SDrA1S7FB_Q3KVAqnIy-MKoQpPrkLXsQIYDoUGYqdie9yAhat_lDOww4p-3Da2f5YnCTngobHeRn-5TP2ztcGsRd3H3TLgSBvHCmzEvsxCec7y3aY9QXpq17yuYHlZDgzvW2-M-yaudXAsnPiI8DNI7edgIc9U-1YxNZMPCY/s320/2x-Picture%209.PNG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEga8F95aDy7a_n56G2zWA4SDrA1S7FB_Q3KVAqnIy-MKoQpPrkLXsQIYDoUGYqdie9yAhat_lDOww4p-3Da2f5YnCTngobHeRn-5TP2ztcGsRd3H3TLgSBvHCmzEvsxCec7y3aY9QXpq17yuYHlZDgzvW2-M-yaudXAsnPiI8DNI7edgIc9U-1YxNZMPCY/s2048/2x-Picture%209.PNG)

I converted it to build under CodeWarrior Pro 7 which is my preferred environment for classic Mac work, and rigged it so that it would display a quick window to show you it was working, do its work, and then terminate back to the Finder. When placed in the Startup Items folder, it will do this job every boot automatically, or can be run on demand. If the input device and output device are both 

ttya, it resets them back to the default 

kbd (ADB keyboard) and 

screen (onboard 54M30 video), and installs an 

nvramrc of its own. The critical code looks like this, using a library function I transplated to do the NVRAM patching in place:

patchstr(21, "kbd");
patchstr(22, "screen");
nvvals[7].word_val = 1; // belt and suspenders approach
patchstr(25,
    "0 to my-self\015"
    "dev /bandit/gc/mace\015"
    "1 encode-int \" PLSCCPort\" property\015"
    "device-end\015"
    "?cr \" Pre-production patches on.\" type\015"
);

The numbers are fixed indexes into NVRAM since this is just a hack, but in order are input-device, output-device, use-nvramrc? and nvramrc itself. This simple nvramrc patches up the Ethernet to work correctly with the Mac OS Apple Enet INIT. Prior Macintoshes with Ethernet, including first generation NuBus Power Macs like the [Workgroup Server 9150](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2026/08/mklinux-and-pimped-out-apple-workgroup.html), had a single Ethernet AAUI port, but AAUI was expensive and unpopular and as the industry moved to twisted-pair Apple offered both an 8P8C ("RJ-45") and AAUI port starting with the 9500 — but still using just the single MACE, so only one port was active at a time. For as yet unexplained reasons, the ANS went back to a single AAUI port with no 8P8C/"RJ-45" despite being an evolution of the same platform base.

This means the MACE is connected directly to the (A)AUI port in the ANS, whereas in machines like the 7300, 7500, 8600, 9500, etc., it switches between the AAUI (equivalent to AUI) or an internal MAU to provide the link over twisted-pair. The MACE embedded in CURIO has a register called PLSCC, or the Physical Layer Signaling Configuration Control, which determines which network port is active. In dual-ported machines, the PLSCC value should be 7 (which includes the $01 enable bit), which corresponds to the "General Purpose Serial Interface" to the circuitry where the signal is routed. In the ANS, however, this value should 1, which specifies a direct AUI connection.

The ANS Mac OS ROM internally and explicitly specifies a property PLSCCPort on /bandit/gc/mace with that value of 1. @joevt gets credit here (a) for  discovering that the Apple Enet INIT looks for and if specified uses this property as an override, relying on a platform default if not, and (b) for the magic incantation required to make this property stick when placed in the nvramrc. Since the ANS looks like a Power Mac 9500 to Mac OS, this value must be provided before Apple Enet runs, so since it's not in the 1.1.20.1 ROM we'll provide it ourselves in Open Firmware before the operating system even starts.

This scheme works and solves both the reboot-shutdown and Ethernet problems simultaneously. But what about bringing the system up from a cold start, where this property won't yet have been set? Well, we have a solution for that too!

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg3o5vuVFG8K_0j-JgibgG1H8YdUiuPQtP-DqYPk9vtDIDaNgcHTkSePk8DdMAsKyOc-j2tQiud-2XG7KwkQSotofW0jiLdV2FF62FLGUA9BqD9ocyR1-RtozCO4uOwzPbwrCR7z0SwT1IJUxuX9Zaw5_ac4zZv9AkrKt48_jhPWUf8Fl2lxHxWGxmCIqA/s320/2x-cfrgrsrc.png)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg3o5vuVFG8K_0j-JgibgG1H8YdUiuPQtP-DqYPk9vtDIDaNgcHTkSePk8DdMAsKyOc-j2tQiud-2XG7KwkQSotofW0jiLdV2FF62FLGUA9BqD9ocyR1-RtozCO4uOwzPbwrCR7z0SwT1IJUxuX9Zaw5_ac4zZv9AkrKt48_jhPWUf8Fl2lxHxWGxmCIqA/s2048/2x-cfrgrsrc.png)

  

The Mac OS 

NameRegistryLib allows us to directly manipulate the Name Registry (which will necessarily have a copy of our Open Firmware properties), so we can also get this property installed during boot as long as we do so before the Apple Enet 

INIT opens. We could do this with an 

ndrv, but we have a simpler and more conventional way which I talked about in this blog before with ways to [expand virtual Mac device support in QEMU](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2022/07/a-brief-dive-into-power-mac-inits-and.html). 

[kanjitalk755's tablet INIT](https://github.com/kanjitalk755/macos9-usb-tablet) installs a handler for USB HID devices during startup which allows QEMU absolute pointer positioning to work with its synthesized virtual USB tablet.

In this INIT, a block of 68K code (remember, the normal state of the Power Macintosh nanokernel is to run 68K code in the emulator) invoked at load time displays the icon and uses the Code Fragment Manager to pull a single non-static PowerPC function from the "PPC " resource (yes, P P C and a trailing space), set up a Universal Procedure Pointer to it as PowerPC native code, and run it. This code fragment is what installs the HID report handler.

Because this extension is so modular in design, we can just gut it and replace the PPC  resource with our own code (yes, PowerPC code can run from resources, not just from the data fork), though I also manually patched the 68K section with a couple NOP instructions to not bother displaying the icon since we don't really need to. This is the entirety of the PowerPC code:

#include <MacErrors.h>
#include <NameRegistry.h>

// MACE Fixer for Shiner ROM 1.1.20.1
// (C)2026 Cameron Kaiser, all rights reserved
// MIT license
// oldvcr.blogspot.com

#define AIX "Devices:device-tree:packages:aix-boot"
#define MACE "Devices:device-tree:bandit:gc:mace"
#define PLSCCPORT "PLSCCPort"

// Any other function must be declared static!
void main(void) {
	OSErr err;
	RegEntryID regEntryID;

	// Ensure this is an ANS ROM that can boot AIX (2.0 doesn't, but doesn't need this)
	err = RegistryCStrEntryLookup(NULL, AIX, &regEntryID);
	if (err != noErr) {
		return;
	}

	// Find MACE and set the PLSCCPort property on it if not already done.
	err = RegistryCStrEntryLookup(NULL, MACE, &regEntryID);
	if (err == noErr) {
		RegPropertyValueSize s; 
		err = RegistryPropertyGetSize(&regEntryID, PLSCCPORT, &s);
		if (err == nrNotFoundErr) { /* may not be found if nvram patches not on */
			UInt32 port = 1;
			err = RegistryPropertyCreate(&regEntryID, PLSCCPORT, &port, sizeof(UInt32));
		}
	}
}

Notice the device tree paths for the two devices we're interested in, Devices:device-tree:packages:aix-boot (or, as an Open Firmware path, /packages/aix-boot) and Devices:device-tree:bandit:gc:mace (/bandit/gc/mace). We don't need to know anything else about what these nodes are or how they're connected to query and modify them. The first step this function takes is to see if this is an AIX-capable ROM by checking for the AIX booter package as a Name Registry node, and if this package isn't present, such as a regular Power Mac or the ANS Mac OS ROM, then we exit. The second step is to see if the PLSCCPort property already exists; if it does, such as being set from our nvramrc, we exit also, or otherwise set the proper value of 1.

Since the whole scheme can only work if our extension runs first, we give it the special file type of scri instead of INIT, which is notionally a WorldScript extension but can be used to load any sort of extension, because WorldScript extensions load before all other INITs (Apple Enet is an INIT). Failing that, the name of the extension (ANS MACE Fixer) is intentionally chosen to lexically sort above Apple Enet so that it will also run first. The upshot is that the property will be set one way or another before the Ethernet INIT runs, and with this extension installed, now the only circumstance where our Ethernet *won't* work would be on the very first boot after a PRAM zap *with extensions off* — which would obviously be an uncommon situation.

It is also important to ensure that main() is the *only* non-static function in the code fragment because of the way the 68K code finds, declares and calls it (see [the prior article](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/2022/07/a-brief-dive-into-power-mac-inits-and.html) for why). CodeWarrior's project settings can be set to build this file as a resource and after doing so we manually merge everything together in ResEdit for the final extension.

As our last stop before the installation instructions, let me also talk a little bit about something *not* in this version of the extensions pack.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj7i5TQDqL4QapyBOsd9JVzTZrBw6PLzQ4zhsXLw9U9p1grrQgdIrDyGCFhRHfV9mSP16LWPcp258VdnWRDx9dm699e3fHEPNZ_mvTQ7cp5OmF2D0XgjCF4CbpriO2hnzhOICkyfLcHtZnRKUOGe60POBPO4VgKd2pAE9uQgekMgIYF30mzm8BFK74wxgU/s320/romfiend-5.png)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj7i5TQDqL4QapyBOsd9JVzTZrBw6PLzQ4zhsXLw9U9p1grrQgdIrDyGCFhRHfV9mSP16LWPcp258VdnWRDx9dm699e3fHEPNZ_mvTQ7cp5OmF2D0XgjCF4CbpriO2hnzhOICkyfLcHtZnRKUOGe60POBPO4VgKd2pAE9uQgekMgIYF30mzm8BFK74wxgU/s3582/romfiend-5.png)

The NCR 53C825 Fast'n'Wide SCSI-2 controller also has its own 

ndrv in the ANS Mac OS ROM. Indeed, it must, or else the internal SCSI wouldn't be bootable with that ROM (the production and pre-production ROMs have their own support and hand everything over to AIX after boot). It is possible to extract this 

ndrv and wrap it as an extension in the same way. It won't be bootable, of course, but in theory this should allow devices on the internal SCSI to be used once Mac OS has booted from the external SCSI. Go ahead and try it. It doesn't work. The machine will boot, but no devices are visible from the internal SCSI drive bays.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjK4KXmEpCZr9d9wh9sYXXWB6vno98sZXt5eGy3ZC_dpZqYClNaqdKQaGWzkervKkGBkwEuc_OfIk5i7oI3wUFmLCH47lt7tIH994BzuuOyt3RcNfSG8jHNrIDYL6QcUTrjCz7g9Ztndu_Jr1XmNw2qFyM-gpqu_hfIOECPrZsdi2VcYzGB2nIyyVJQx3Y/s320/2x-Picture%203.PNG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjK4KXmEpCZr9d9wh9sYXXWB6vno98sZXt5eGy3ZC_dpZqYClNaqdKQaGWzkervKkGBkwEuc_OfIk5i7oI3wUFmLCH47lt7tIH994BzuuOyt3RcNfSG8jHNrIDYL6QcUTrjCz7g9Ztndu_Jr1XmNw2qFyM-gpqu_hfIOECPrZsdi2VcYzGB2nIyyVJQx3Y/s2048/2x-Picture%203.PNG)

Apple PCI DDK 3.0 also includes a utility (

Load Driver Test) where you can test the structure of an 

ndrv to see if it's valid (useful for hardware builders before they spend a lot of money burning defective ROMs). This utility basically checks if the 

ndrv can be loaded as a code fragment, and if it can, that it has a sensible driver description block, and shows the device node it's looking for and the driver name it installs.

We can immediately see from this that the node name is wrong. In the ANS Mac OS 2.0 ROM, the 53C825 nodes in the Name Registry are named apple53C8xx, not 53c825 as they are in the pre-production ROM. Triumphantly I changed the string and length byte to make the matched name 53c825. It still didn't work.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEino7Krk6YQIsOIUVosPzQa_k5BDgicwpzWuTwvs6cyS4PdnXsBvl1H0p58KLXVwRZ9voJRyXlLLooHP86ansU1eckG2UMWp-ct65oiNYBqnOFSN3HzA84xzt5NktbRTf6AGd_sCXVAKvX5XXQamyEIi2FBrUTuaWB4amHvNQNjXghVjTxyY9_OL0gY-Tg/s320/2x-Picture%204.PNG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEino7Krk6YQIsOIUVosPzQa_k5BDgicwpzWuTwvs6cyS4PdnXsBvl1H0p58KLXVwRZ9voJRyXlLLooHP86ansU1eckG2UMWp-ct65oiNYBqnOFSN3HzA84xzt5NktbRTf6AGd_sCXVAKvX5XXQamyEIi2FBrUTuaWB4amHvNQNjXghVjTxyY9_OL0gY-Tg/s2048/2x-Picture%204.PNG)

The PCI DDK has an additional tool (

PCIPeek) which allows you to mess around with PCI-based devices. When we ask it for the PCI configuration space for one of the 53C825s using the node name 

53c825, we can pull it up and see all 64 bytes are valid. Though the 

compatible name doesn't [fetch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pubd-spHN-0), this does at least prove that the issue isn't the logic board and the node name is correct.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh-3QF9u8tJyTDGfQW9BqLQ77KSQf982rkIRv5LSW0sdkAoZu3vFJh36zaNI2cdEtT2aV_inN4BCbi6tLliRrL16Tx5SLnuMOWR3LSRhJD9wiRxFpUSD2jG9ePs4zv4qhllwXy9ZtCLooSepot1AripsyiYdWNnMoT_8_WsG5YkJm8SsLUOf_HCd7y_zos/s320/romfiend-7.png)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh-3QF9u8tJyTDGfQW9BqLQ77KSQf982rkIRv5LSW0sdkAoZu3vFJh36zaNI2cdEtT2aV_inN4BCbi6tLliRrL16Tx5SLnuMOWR3LSRhJD9wiRxFpUSD2jG9ePs4zv4qhllwXy9ZtCLooSepot1AripsyiYdWNnMoT_8_WsG5YkJm8SsLUOf_HCd7y_zos/s3334/romfiend-7.png)

The next step was to look at the driver description in the hex editor. This is again another trivially compressed PEF. Like any well-behaved SCSI driver, it implements a fully-specified SIM (SCSI Interface Module), which, according to the SCSI Common Access Method (CAM), is the link between the 53C825 host bus adapter (HBA) and the transport (XPT) layer that in turn hooks into the SCSI drivers used by the operating system. You should be able to see the device node name and the Macintosh driver name, but the byte before the Pascal string for the Mac driver name here is $04. Unlike video 

ndrvs, the documentation states SCSI 

ndrvs should only have a single bit set in that byte, in this case specifying that the family expert handles loading the driver (

kDriverIsUnderExpertControl, $04).

Since that didn't load nor open the driver, I tried setting various bit combinations of forcing it to load upon discovery and/or open upon load, all of which ended up hanging the ANS doing boot. Remember how I said that SHIFT doesn't stop ndrvs from loading? Each of these permutations thus ended up making the external SCSI volume unbootable until the poison ndrv was removed. I had to connect it to the WallStreet PowerBook G3 (it was handy) to get it out, though as a check I had the Wally boot from the same volume just to see what it would do — and it booted fine. The driver doesn't load on the Wally almost certainly because the device name doesn't match anything, which also implies the hang is specific to trying to bring up the device on the ANS or we'd hang on the Wally too.

This leaves us at the mercy of the family expert, so the next thing I tried was various combinations of service category and type. By default this is ndrvgenr, so I tried ndrvscsi, ndrvblok, blokgenr, blokscsi, scsigenr, scsiblok, scsiscsi, blokblok and finally an intemperate combination inappropriate for a family blog, and while none of these locked up the 700, none of them made any difference either.

After all that I'm not sure this approach would have worked for getting the internal SCSI bus working anyway, at least not without additional code. Apple's PCI documentation says, "The SCSI expert is simpler than some other experts" and while it mentions the situation of a "PCI card that wants to register a SIM with the SCSI Manager" which necessarily covers the situation of one in ROM, it says nothing about disk-based drivers. It's possible the SCSI expert just doesn't handle this situation because a non-bootable SCSI bus is certainly less useful, and while we could write up an INIT to try loading the SIM manually, I'm still pondering how this would work and I have yet to find a working disk-based driver for a 53C825-based card that I could hack as an alternative (suggestions solicited in the comments). The PCI DDK 3.0 notably includes a "driver" for this chipset, but only to let you mess around with the hardware — it's intentionally not structured as a SIM, so it wouldn't be an effective foundation.

But you can still try the other pieces, so let's pick up with the install instructions now that you have the prerequisites.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi-wrPrtVrTRYK8SqAYW5QXb7jjBEimdJ2dSRRtpaCd_P3VltZk4c9EJ-OyA9FNdxrlPuVRZ3OzICVYfif8y7VxYMWkmnxdugsHM3NrFcbpZeLWgAjLU2p1rnzRTDd59tMNQd2PLhceotkBuILBHFX8zAhOJuHPZaaXH_cBKwGZ3XcMli3VWz6s6A0jvQA/s320/PXL_20261013_011603055.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi-wrPrtVrTRYK8SqAYW5QXb7jjBEimdJ2dSRRtpaCd_P3VltZk4c9EJ-OyA9FNdxrlPuVRZ3OzICVYfif8y7VxYMWkmnxdugsHM3NrFcbpZeLWgAjLU2p1rnzRTDd59tMNQd2PLhceotkBuILBHFX8zAhOJuHPZaaXH_cBKwGZ3XcMli3VWz6s6A0jvQA/s4080/PXL_20261013_011603055.jpg)

If you were working with a pre-built Mac OS disk image, using the system you used to build it put the ANS MACE Fixer and ANS Video Enabler into the Extensions folder, and the ANS Startup Fixer into the Startup Items folder. If you are doing the install on the ANS itself, simply have the CD disk image ready to go on your external device (or connect a real physical external SCSI CD-ROM).

Assuming you didn't tl;dr this article, your depowered logic board should now be fully reset. Close the drawer and lock the rear key and plug the server back in, then plug in ADB and your SCSI device. Remove all hard drives from the front; you can't boot MacOS from them anyway, and it will simply confuse Open Firmware. The CD-ROM and any tape drives may remain, though do note they currently won't work either. Connect your display to the *on-board* VGA port, not to any PCI video card, and finally power on the system. If you are using one of Jeff's current replica ROMs, you may need to hit Control-Command-Reset after powering up to get the bong (this is an electrical issue we're sorting out). From a cold start with no bootable AIX volume, the 1.1.20.1 ROM will automatically bomb into Open Firmware, showing you the prompt here. If you don't see this screen, make sure your monitor is connected to the onboard port.

If you've already prepared your external Mac OS volume and the extensions are in their proper places, just type bye at the Open Firmware ok prompt. You will see the message

/AAPL,ROM
MacOS is currently unsupported, use at your own risk.

while the ROM component looks for your startup disk. Once it finds it, there will be a pause, then the screen will flash and drop into the Mac OS mid-boot. Remember, the Startup Fixer must run *once every time Mac OS starts up*, or your system will come up with a black screen on the next boot. You can manually fix this by entering Open Firmware with a serial connection to Port 2 (38400bps, 8-N-1) and enter setenv input-device kbd, setenv output-device screen, setenv use-nvramrc? false and reset all, or you can just reset the logic board.

If you are doing an install from an external Mac OS CD-ROM or CD image, *move your display to the PCI video card* and then *blindly* type bye. You will get the Mac 50% dithered grey, then a Happy Mac, then the CD should start. Install Mac OS as usual to your previously prepared blank disk image. After the installation completes, if you can, install the extensions (e.g., from a floppy disk or via AppleShare over LocalTalk) and startup item as described above *before you shut down*. Either way, shut down, power off and reset your logic board again, disable or remove the CD-ROM/image, move the display back to the onboard video port, and power back on to the Open Firmware prompt. If the extensions were installed, just type bye — you're good to go. If you couldn't, move the display to the PCI card again, blindly type bye, bring up Mac OS from your external volume, install the extensions, shut down, power off and reset your logic board one last time, then move the display back to the onboard video port. *Now* you can boot by just typing bye also.

[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhRDIMLLXGNfMcBRRqNse3QWZPktv2w-LAE2lRnuNsLeG_OyGpVn_Il4SavVHo2guVyanuRYAqeM5DliggNcY7QrmtP2D2RHvxU_T_x8RAmMMMn3sP4McBNv3dE2Hp7-d8B3lUy0hsEonXNcoVC0bhlrHX4vuU5jpgmxrm48YNamqlC1Cnt7jomxP9vj1s/s320/2x-Picture%205.PNG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhRDIMLLXGNfMcBRRqNse3QWZPktv2w-LAE2lRnuNsLeG_OyGpVn_Il4SavVHo2guVyanuRYAqeM5DliggNcY7QrmtP2D2RHvxU_T_x8RAmMMMn3sP4McBNv3dE2Hp7-d8B3lUy0hsEonXNcoVC0bhlrHX4vuU5jpgmxrm48YNamqlC1Cnt7jomxP9vj1s/s2048/2x-Picture%205.PNG)

Things still to do:

- Get the internal SCSI bays working, which may require us to create a modified ROM and put the ndrv there with the proper node name. However, one other possibility is by installing a MacOS-bootable SCSI PCI card. The Shiner logic board has 68-pin connectors on the logic board that directly feed into the two front SCSI busses (bus 0 controls the top four trays and bus 1 controls the bottom three and the 700's rear two). These connectors were intended for the ANS PCI RAID card, but I don't see why we couldn't just connect a regular controller there as long as we change its SCSI ID to not conflict with the 53C825, which should be possible on Adaptec cards with the PowerDomain Control CDEV. I intend to do some experimentation with that, including finding an optimum card which is Mac-bootable (or flashable to same) and supports full Fast'n'Wide SCSI-2, yet is *not* supported by AIX so that the regular 53C825 will "just work."

- On a reboot, the ANS may go into its Long RAM Test. This is not only *not* fatal but is arguably intended behaviour and it will start normally afterwards, though the delay is annoying. On the other hand, even though the ANS Mac OS ROM doesn't do this, it also doesn't properly register the sticks as parity RAM even if they are. I don't know if I can fix this by tweaking Open Firmware or this requires a ROM patch, though I suspect it's the latter. In the meantime, you can manually cut it short by hitting Control-Command-Reset.

Hopefully you'll see solutions to one or both of these in [a future article](https://oldvcr.blogspot.com/search/label/ans). For now, you can get everything on [the Github repo](https://github.com/classilla/ansmac), including source code for CodeWarrior Pro 7. Note that this compiler cannot build the 68K portion of the ANS MACE Fixer, but I've included the source for that too, and you don't need to build the 68K segment anyway merely to modify the PowerPC portion. Each portion is under its own license and you should read the brief notes. No AI was used.
